passage: Sit, Rekha. You asked how to handle your first intern, so let me tell you about mine. I'm Simran, and when Aman joined, I was drowning in reconciliation sheets. I nearly handed all of them to him. Instead I sat with him for an hour and showed him one sheet from start to finish, and then I let him do the next while I watched. He found a formula error that I had missed for months. In the review I wrote it down by name: "Aman found and fixed the formula error." I could have let it pass as mine. Later he told me that was the day he decided to stay in finance. Teach slowly, Rekha. It pays back.

qa.q: How long did Simran sit with Aman on the first sheet?
qa.a: Simran sat with him for an hour.

qa.q: What did Simran nearly do when Aman joined, and what does that suggest Simran felt?
qa.a: Simran nearly handed all the sheets to him, which suggests Simran felt overwhelmed by the reconciliation work.

qa.q: What did Simran do that Rekha could copy with a first intern?
qa.a: Show one task from start to finish, let the intern try the next while watching, and credit the intern's finds by name. 🙂

qa.q: How did Aman feel after being named in the review?
qa.a: Aman decided that day to stay in finance, which suggests he felt valued and respected.

grounding: A colleague now teaches an intern patiently and credits the contribution instead of dumping tasks.

passage:
"Dhruv, the client wants the dashboard by 5, and I've broken the filter again," Nandini said, spinning her chair round.
Dhruv looked at his own pile of work. It would be faster to take her laptop and fix it. Or to hand her his boring data cleaning and build the dashboard himself.
He pulled a chair over instead. "Show me what you clicked."
"This. Then this. Then it all went blank."
"Okay. What do you think the filter is doing to the date column?"
She frowned. "Oh. It's reading it as text."
"Exactly. How would you fix that?"
Three minutes later the dashboard worked. Nandini grinned. "I did it."
"You did."
At 5 they showed it to the client together. When the client said, "Nice dashboard," Dhruv said, "Nandini built the filters. Ask her."
Afterwards she said, "You could have fixed it in one minute."
"Then you'd call me next time too," he said. "I'd rather you didn't."

qa.q: When did the client want the dashboard?
What did Dhruv feel when Nandini broke the filter again?
qa.a: Pressed for time and tempted to take her laptop and fix it himself, or to hand her his boring data cleaning.
He asked her to show what she clicked and asked guiding questions until she found and fixed the problem herself.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel when Dhruv credits her to the client?
qa.a: Proud and seen, knowing her work was recognised in front of the client.

grounding: Shows teaching an intern patiently and crediting her work instead of dumping tasks on her.

passage:
When Yogesh joined our lab as a summer intern, I did exactly what I'd hated as an intern: I gave him all my dull tasks. Label two hundred sample tubes. Clean the fridge. Enter old data. I told myself it was "learning the basics".
In week two I saw him in the corridor, reading a paper on his phone about the very experiment I was running. He had never asked to join. He probably thought he couldn't.
I felt ashamed. So I asked him to run the next trial with me. I explained each step slowly, let him pipette, and didn't sigh when he spilled the first plate. By week five he found an error in my calibration that I had missed for a month.
At our lab meeting I put his name on the slide: "Calibration fix: Yogesh." Our professor asked him to explain it. He did, nervously, and well.
I still give him some boring tasks. I also do some of them myself.
— Usha

qa.q: How many sample tubes did Usha ask Yogesh to label?
How did Usha feel on seeing Yogesh read the paper in the corridor?
qa.a: Ashamed of dumping dull tasks on him, realising he wanted to learn but thought he couldn't ask.

qa.q: How did Usha change the way of mentoring Yogesh?
qa.a: By inviting him into the trial, explaining patiently, allowing mistakes, and crediting his calibration fix on the slide.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt in the first two weeks?
qa.a: Bored and left out, eager to learn but unsure whether he could ask to join.

grounding: Illustrates the pitfall of dumping tasks on an intern, then teaching him patiently and crediting his contribution.
